meta.purpose: Concept pairs that are routinely confused, with the discriminator that separates them and the trap the exam uses to exploit the confusion.
meta.why_here: The mapping to bank questions lives in this file rather than as tags across 292 question files. One place to review, cheap to extend, and adding a pair later touches nothing else.
meta.uses: Feeds effectiveness checking (does drilling a pair precede improved accuracy on the questions that turn on it) and will seed a future Pair Split game.
meta.note: question_ids may be empty. An empty list is a genuine coverage gap in the bank, not an oversight.

pairs.label: RTO vs RPO
pairs.discriminator: RTO looks FORWARD from the disruption: how long until service is restored. RPO looks BACKWARD: how much recent data you can afford to lose.
pairs.trap: A stem gives a backup frequency and asks which objective it satisfies. Backup interval is the data at risk, so it is RPO. Restoration speed is RTO.

pairs.label: Incident vs problem management
pairs.discriminator: Incident management RESTORES SERVICE as fast as possible, accepting a workaround. Problem management ELIMINATES THE CAUSE so it stops recurring.
pairs.trap: The same outage recurs many times, each closed quickly on restoration. Fast incident response looks like success; the finding is that no problem management exists.

pairs.label: Shared-key MAC vs digital signature
pairs.discriminator: A shared key means EITHER party could have produced the value, so there is NO nonrepudiation. Only a private key binds the message to one signer.
pairs.trap: A party denies sending something. A MAC is offered as an option and looks cryptographically respectable, but it cannot settle a dispute between the two key holders.

pairs.label: Which key, and for what
pairs.discriminator: Encrypt with the RECIPIENT'S PUBLIC key for confidentiality (only they can open it). Sign with the SENDER'S PRIVATE key for authentication, integrity and nonrepudiation.
pairs.trap: The stem asks for one property and the distractors offer the operation that delivers the other.

pairs.label: IDS vs IPS
pairs.discriminator: Placement decides capability. A sensor on a mirror or SPAN port receives a COPY after delivery and can only alert. Only an INLINE device can drop traffic.
pairs.trap: The stem says 'stop traffic before it reaches the server'. An IDS option describes good monitoring, which is irrelevant to the stated requirement.

pairs.label: Incremental vs differential backup
pairs.discriminator: Incremental: changes since the LAST BACKUP OF ANY TYPE. Small and fast to take, SLOW to restore (full plus every incremental in order). Differential: changes since the last FULL. Grows daily, FAST to restore (full plus one).
pairs.trap: The trade-off is inverted between backup time and restore time, so an answer that is right about one is wrong about the other.

pairs.label: Inherent / control / detection / residual risk
pairs.discriminator: Inherent: before any controls. Control: controls fail to catch it. Detection: the AUDITOR'S procedures fail to find it. Residual: what is left after controls operate. Detection risk is the only one the auditor controls, by doing more work.
pairs.trap: High control risk requires MORE substantive testing, not less. The intuitive-sounding answer is backwards.

pairs.label: Compliance vs substantive testing
pairs.discriminator: Compliance asks whether the CONTROL operated. Substantive asks whether the DATA is right, regardless of what the controls did.
pairs.trap: Distractors offer real-sounding distinctions (who performs it, whether sampling is used) that are not the actual difference.

pairs.label: Design vs operating effectiveness deficiency
pairs.discriminator: Design: would NOT achieve the objective even if performed perfectly. Operating: sound design, but not performed consistently. Different remedies follow.
pairs.trap: Policies, approvals and certificates are DESIGN evidence. Evidence that a control ran over a period is OPERATING evidence. Stems ask for one and offer the other.

pairs.label: Policy / standard / procedure / guideline
pairs.discriminator: Policy: mandatory intent, broad. Standard: mandatory SPECIFICS (which algorithm, what key length). Procedure: step-by-step how-to. Guideline: advisory. Baseline: minimum configuration for a class of system.
pairs.trap: A policy that mandates something with no standard beneath it is untestable. The missing document is almost always the standard.

pairs.label: Data owner / custodian / steward
pairs.discriminator: Owner: business, DECIDES classification and accepts risk. Custodian: usually IT, STORES and protects it. Steward: does the day-to-day quality, definition and access administration on the owner's behalf.
pairs.trap: Classification decisions are offered to IT or to security. Both hold the data; neither owns the judgment about its sensitivity.

pairs.label: BIA vs risk assessment
pairs.discriminator: A BIA is THREAT-AGNOSTIC: what happens as an outage lengthens, regardless of cause. A risk assessment identifies and rates the threats themselves.
pairs.trap: Distractors describe threat identification, which sounds like the obvious first step but belongs to the risk assessment.

pairs.label: Certificate expiry vs revocation
pairs.discriminator: Ordinary validation already catches EXPIRED certificates. Only revocation checking catches a certificate that is still within its validity period but belongs to a COMPROMISED KEY or a departed user.
pairs.trap: 'Expired certificates will be accepted' is offered as the risk of not checking revocation. It is not; expiry is checked anyway.

pairs.label: Risk appetite / tolerance / capacity
pairs.discriminator: Appetite: how much risk the organization is WILLING to take pursuing its objectives. Tolerance: acceptable variation around that. Capacity: how much it could ABSORB before failing.
pairs.trap: Residual risk and maximum possible loss are offered as definitions of appetite. Appetite is a chosen position, not a measured quantity.

pairs.label: Vulnerability scan vs penetration test
pairs.discriminator: A scan ENUMERATES known weaknesses individually and rates them in isolation. A pen test CHAINS them to demonstrate whether a real path to a target exists.
pairs.trap: The stem asks whether several minor weaknesses could be COMBINED. Only the pen test answers a question about combination.

pairs.label: Preventive / detective / corrective / compensating
pairs.discriminator: Preventive stops it happening. Detective finds it after. Corrective restores afterward. Compensating substitutes for a control that cannot be implemented. Directive instructs behavior.
pairs.trap: When a stem asks what BEST ADDRESSES a weakness, preventive usually wins. When it asks about recovery or evidence, that ranking inverts.

pairs.label: Parallel / phased / direct changeover
pairs.discriminator: Parallel: run both, compare outputs. Safest, most expensive, heaviest staff burden. Phased: by module or location, contains risk, needs interim interfaces. Direct: fastest, cheapest, NO FALLBACK.
pairs.trap: 'Parallel is cheapest' and 'direct takes longest' are both inversions of the truth, and both appear as distractors.

pairs.label: Hot / warm / cold / reciprocal site
pairs.discriminator: Hot: equipped, configured, current data — fastest and dearest. Warm: hardware and connectivity, no current data. Cold: space and power only. Reciprocal: depends entirely on a partner's readiness at the moment of need.
pairs.trap: Reciprocal agreements look cheap and cooperative. The weakness is that both parties drift, and a regional event affects both.

pairs.label: IaaS / PaaS / SaaS responsibility split
pairs.discriminator: The split of TASKS moves with the service model. ACCOUNTABILITY for the data never moves — the customer remains data owner in every model.
pairs.trap: Options list operational tasks (patching, physical security, hypervisor config) that all belong to the provider. The one that stays is accountability for the data and who may access it.

pairs.label: Authentication factors
pairs.discriminator: Multifactor requires factors of DIFFERENT TYPES. Password plus security questions is one factor twice. Two biometrics is multimodal, not multifactor.
pairs.trap: Every distractor is a plausible-looking combination that is actually single-factor.

pairs.label: Change / release / configuration management
pairs.discriminator: Change: should this change be made, and who approved it. Release: packaging, scheduling and deploying an approved bundle. Configuration: the record of what exists and what depends on what.
pairs.trap: All three are legitimate-sounding answers to any question about controlling production, so read which activity the stem actually describes.

pairs.label: Quality assurance vs quality control
pairs.discriminator: QA works on the PROCESS to prevent defects. QC inspects the DELIVERABLE to detect them. Preventive versus detective, one level up.
pairs.trap: Timing-based distinctions ('QA happens at the end') are offered and are wrong; QA runs throughout.

pairs.label: KPI vs KRI
pairs.discriminator: A KPI measures how well an objective IS BEING achieved — it looks back at outcomes. A KRI is FORWARD-LOOKING signal that exposure is building before the loss occurs.
pairs.trap: Organizations report KPIs and neglect KRIs, so the exam asks which one gives early warning.

pairs.label: Data controller vs processor
pairs.discriminator: The CONTROLLER determines the purposes and means of processing and carries primary accountability. The processor acts on the controller's instructions and carries its own security obligations.
pairs.trap: Size or technical sophistication is offered as the distinction. Neither is relevant — it is about who decides.

pairs.label: Resilience vs disaster recovery
pairs.discriminator: Resilience ABSORBS component failure so the service never becomes unavailable. Disaster recovery begins where resilience ended, once the service has actually been lost.
pairs.trap: Recovery-flavoured answers (alternate site, offsite backups, restoring within RTO) are offered as definitions of resilience.

pairs.label: Continuity test types
pairs.discriminator: Assurance and operational risk rise together: checklist, tabletop, parallel, full interruption. Only full interruption proves the organization can run without the primary environment, which is why it can cause a real outage.
pairs.trap: The stem asks for greatest assurance AND greatest risk together. They are the same answer, which feels wrong.

pairs.label: Verification vs validation
pairs.discriminator: Verification: are we building it RIGHT (against the specification). Validation: are we building the RIGHT THING (against the business need).
pairs.trap: A system can pass every verification test and still fail validation, because the specification itself was wrong.

pairs.label: FAR / FRR / CER in biometrics
pairs.discriminator: FAR admits the wrong person — the SECURITY failure. FRR blocks the right person — the USABILITY failure. CER is where they meet, and lower CER means a better device.
pairs.trap: Tuning to reduce one raises the other. A stem about security risk wants FAR; one about user complaints wants FRR.

pairs.label: Attribute vs variable vs stop-or-go sampling
pairs.discriminator: Attribute: rate of DEVIATION from a control (yes/no per item), used in compliance testing. Variable: monetary VALUE of misstatement, used substantively. Stop-or-go: staged testing that can end early when few errors are expected.
pairs.trap: Statistical sampling lets you QUANTIFY sampling risk; it does not eliminate it. That distractor appears often.
